name: Washington University in St. Louis

profile.address: 222, South Newstead Avenue, Central West End, Saint Louis, Missouri, 63110
profile.reading:
At 222 South Newstead Avenue in the Central West End of St. Louis, Washington University in St. Louis operates the Genome Data Center, a computing facility built to support the university's McDonnell Genome Institute. The institute, known for most of its history as the Genome Sequencing Center, is one of the most prominent genomics research programs in the United States and was one of a handful of centers that carried out the bulk of the sequencing work for the Human Genome Project in the late 1990s and early 2000s. That project generated enormous volumes of raw sequence data even by the standards of the time, and the demands of storing, processing, and analyzing genomic data at that scale pushed the university toward dedicated computing infrastructure separate from its general campus IT systems.

The Genome Data Center sits a short distance from the McDonnell Genome Institute's main offices at 4444 Forest Park Avenue, on the Washington University School of Medicine's Central West End campus, and functions as the computing backbone for the institute's ongoing work. The Genome Institute continues large scale DNA sequencing today across cancer genomics, infectious disease research, and other areas of biomedical science, and its affiliated Genome Technology Access Center lists computational biology and bioinformatics among the services it offers to researchers, work that depends on sustained, high throughput computing and storage capacity.

Washington University has not published detailed specifications for the building itself. There is no publicly available figure for its square footage, its critical IT power capacity, or its cooling architecture, which is typical for university research computing facilities that serve internal academic and clinical programs rather than outside tenants. Unlike a commercial data center trying to attract customers, a university research computing building has little reason to publish capacity or uptime figures for a public audience, and its scale is generally understood in terms of the science it supports rather than the building's technical specifications. What is publicly documented is its role: a dedicated facility, distinct from the Genome Institute's administrative offices, purpose built to house the computing and storage infrastructure behind one of the country's leading genome sequencing programs.

reading:
Washington University in St. Louis is a private research university, and it appears in a data centre registry for a narrow and specific reason. Its School of Medicine operates a dedicated building for research computing, listed by the medical campus facilities organisation as the Genome Data Center at 222 South Newstead Avenue in the Central West End neighbourhood of St. Louis. That address is confirmed by the university's own facilities directory, and the coordinates stored on this row fall within a block of it, so this is a genuine institutional facility rather than a mistagged office or a stray polygon.

The computing exists because of the research programme it serves. The McDonnell Genome Institute, established in 1993 and known for most of its history as the Genome Sequencing Center, was one of the small number of centres that carried the Human Genome Project, contributing about a quarter of the finished human sequence. In 2008 it became the first to sequence the complete genome of a cancer patient, a woman with leukaemia, and it has drawn more than 1.3 billion dollars in research funding since it was founded. Its offices sit at 4444 Forest Park Avenue, roughly half a mile from the data centre building, and its affiliated access centres offer sequencing, genome engineering, mass spectrometry and computational biology services to researchers. High throughput sequencing produces raw data at volumes that outgrew general campus information technology early, which is the ordinary reason a university ends up owning a purpose built machine room rather than renting rack space.

What the public record does not contain is any of the numbers a commercial data centre publishes. There is no square footage, no critical IT load, no utility service size, no standby generator rating, no fuel reserve and no efficiency figure for this building. The university publishes none of it, and there is no permit, tariff filing or utility docket in the public domain that supplies it. The building is tagged in OpenStreetMap as single storey and university use, which is consistent with a low rise purpose built machine room, but that is a crowd sourced observation rather than a documented specification, and it should not be converted into a capacity estimate.

That absence is the honest finding for this entry rather than a gap to be filled. Academic and medical research computing is a real and substantial category of demand, and it is systematically invisible in commercial capacity databases, because universities do not sell space, do not publish tariffs and have no marketing reason to describe their plant. Where an aggregator does carry a megawatt figure for a facility like this one, it is almost always an estimate produced by inference rather than a number an owner or a regulator ever stated. This registry records the Genome Data Center as confirmed infrastructure with an unpublished capacity, and the operator website field points at the School of Medicine rather than the university as a whole, which is the correct level for a building that serves the medical campus.
